data.title: US judge blocks Trump administration's 'loyalty' question for job applicants
data.description:
US judge blocks Trump administration's 'loyalty' question for job applicants

By Nate Raymond
Sat, 12 September 2026 at 12:10 am UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Nate Raymond

BOSTON, Sept 11 (Reuters) - A federal judge on Friday blocked U.S. President Donald Trump's administration from continuing to ask applicants for civil service jobs throughout the government to respond to ‌what unions described as a partisan "loyalty question."

U.S. District Judge George O'Toole in Boston sided with three ‌unions representing government workers who sued last year after the administration began asking applicants for nonpartisan federal jobs to write essays explaining how ​they would help advance Trump's policies and executive orders.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The unions, including the American Federation of Government Employees, argued the question mandated by the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) unlawfully politicized the hiring process for career government workers by attempting to assess their support for the Republican president.

O'Toole, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the question had been asked of ‌applicants to positions ranging from an ⁠air traffic control specialist to a crane operator to a nuclear materials courier.

He said the unions' members reasonably interpreted it as an attempt to determine the applicants' political views, even ⁠though the Civil Service Reform Act bars making employment decisions for such jobs on the basis of political affiliation.

"The plaintiffs are thus likely to succeed in showing that there is no legitimate governmental interest in inquiring into the political beliefs of ​applicants ​to federal civil service vacancies," O'Toole wrote.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The judge halted the ​use of the question on grounds that it ‌likely violated the Administrative Procedure Act by infringing on speech rights under the U.S. Constitution's First Amendment.

Lawyers for the unions at the liberal group Democracy Forward welcomed the ruling, saying that over 70,000 federal job postings had included the question, undermining what is supposed to be a merit-based hiring system.

"Requiring federal job applicants to answer politically motivated questions goes against the very nature of the nonpartisan civil service," AFGE National President Everett Kelley said in a ‌statement.

The other two unions are the American Federation of State, County ​and Municipal Employees and the National Association of Government Employees.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

OPM did ​not immediately respond to a request for comment. ​It has previously defended the question as optional and said that it had been clear ‌that hiring decisions could not be based on ​political beliefs.

It had adopted the ​question in response to an executive order Trump signed in January 2025 that required it to develop a hiring plan that brought into the federal workforce "only highly skilled Americans dedicated to the furtherance of ​American ideals, values, and interests."

OPM in ‌a May 2025 memo to the heads of all executive agencies set forth various actions to implement ​Trump's order, including by requiring that job applicants be asked to respond to the essay ​question.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Tom Hogue)

data.title: Police investigate death of Tasia Fortune, found hanging from tree, as a homicide
data.description:
Police investigate death of Tasia Fortune, found hanging from tree, as a homicide

Chris Boyette, CNN
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 11:03 pm UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Jackson, Mississippi, police are investigating the death of Tasia Fortune as a homicide after the 29-year-old Black woman was found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned house last month, the city's police chief said Tuesday.

"Jackson Police Department has been investigating this case from day one as a homicide, until we hear otherwise from the medical examiner's office," Chief RaShall Brackney said at a city council meeting.

Police had previously categorized the case as a "death pending investigation."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

With the autopsy results pending, Fortune's family is demanding answers and local officials are questioning the circumstances surrounding the case.

The scrutiny is unfolding against Mississippi's long history of racial violence involving hangings and follows other recent hanging deaths in the state that authorities ruled were suicides.

"We need to pursue (Fortune's) investigation to its final conclusion and whatever the results, we need to address those results," Jackson City Council President Vernon Hartley said.

The police chief addressed the city council after a letter written by Christy Spivey, Fortune's mother, was read aloud at the meeting.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I have no more answers from one day of this investigation," Spivey wrote. "The detectives are like they are on a prerecorded message, just saying the same thing over and over. And now it's gone to silence."

unknown content item

-

On Thursday, Spivey said in a post on the family's GoFundMe page that she had asked Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes for help "because of the silence and rudeness of Jackson Police Department."

"Thanks to him putting Tasia's case on for the council meeting Jackson Police department finally came out and admitted that they were treating this as a homicide which I had already known that but the public didn't personally know," Spivey wrote.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Investigators have remained in regular contact with Spivey and her husband, but are awaiting the ruling from the medical examiner's office, Brackney said.

CNN has reached out to Spivey for comment.

The Mississippi State Medical Examiner's Office conducted an autopsy on Fortune on August 11, but police have not yet received the results, Brackney told the council.

The chief said she had been in contact with the director of the medical examiner's office as well as the commissioner who oversees it but has not been able to get a ruling on the cause and manner of Fortune's death.

"Autopsy reports are not considered outstanding or backlogged until they have exceeded 90 days," and the average turnaround time for the Mississippi Department of Public Safety, which oversees the state medical examiner's office, is less than that, spokesperson Alex Gibert told CNN on Thursday.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"The Mississippi Department of Public Safety does not comment on the status or findings of individual autopsy reports. Autopsy reports can take time to complete as the State Medical Examiner's Office gathers and reviews all necessary testing, findings, and other information before a report is finalized," Gibert said in a statement.

The department referred CNN to the Jackson Police Department and the Hinds County Coroner.

CNN has reached out to the medical examiner's office for more information.

There have been no arrests made in relation to Fortune's death, police told CNN in August, but the father of one of Fortune's children was arrested shortly after the discovery of her body on unrelated weapons charges. He is still in custody, jail records show.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Fortune's "children have their future secured" as the family continues "working on justice," Spivey said in the GoFundMe post.

Brackney warned people not to jump to conclusions before all the results are in.

"There is a lot of misinformation out there about this case and other ones," she said.

Stokes called for answers, especially considering the violent history of race relations in Mississippi and several other hangings in the state.

He said people in his ward are worried and want to know what happened to Fortune.

"They're concerned because they're saying no answers have been given as to what happened, who did what, or anything else, and everybody wants to know what happened," Stokes told CNN affiliate WAPT.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The investigation into Fortune's death comes less than a year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused white man in his 30s, in Vicksburg, according to The Associated Press. Both deaths were determined by authorities to be suicides.

"Hanging is an ugly, ugly part of our past that we never, ever want to come back again," Stokes said at the city council meeting.

The council member also told CNN affiliate WLBT the delay in answers about Fortune's death raises questions about the investigation.

"It sends the message that you're trying to hide something, and we do not need to hide anything in the state of Mississippi. We want the world to know we're open and above board," he said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN's Cindy Von Quednow and Leah Thomeer contributed to this report.

data.title: Putin says events in Europe, like AfD's win in Germany, caused by Western globalists
data.description:
Putin says events in Europe, like AfD's win in Germany, caused by Western globalists

Reuters
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 11:22 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Sept 11 (Reuters) - Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Friday that events in Europe, including the far-right victory in a German state election, were the ‌result of "system errors" committed by globalists in the West.

Putin, speaking to reporters ‌in a pool report on the first day of a visit to India, also said the conflict in ​Ukraine was the fault of the West for constantly putting pressure on Moscow and seeking to "drag" Ukraine into the NATO alliance.

The Russian president said he would offer no comment on Sunday's top result for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt, ‌but then added that Western ⁠elites were to blame for events on the continent, including the election.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I think that everything happening in Europe right now is basically the ⁠result of system errors by the so-called West ... the Western globalists in politics, security, and economics," Putin said.

Western countries, he said, had also disregarded Russia's opposition to NATO's eastward expansion.

After a ​Russia-friendly president ​was forced to flee Ukraine in 2014, ​he said the West "immediately set the ‌goal of dragging Ukraine into NATO. And this ultimately turned out to be the main reason for today's tragic events in Ukraine."

"It is the Western globalist elites that are to blame for this, though they keep shifting the blame onto us all the time."

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"People in Europe, I think, understand what is going on," he told reporters. "Hence, today's results ‌in Germany and tendencies in Europe as a ​whole."

Western countries, he said, were "scaring their people with a ​fake threat from Russia, supposedly arising ​since the times of the Soviet Union. But there is no ‌such threat and there never has been."

Putin ​is to attend a ​BRICS summit from Saturday in India, along with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian.

The AfD came first in last Sunday's election after promising ​to curb migration and restore ‌ties with Moscow. The AfD must now attract defectors from other parties ​or reach an agreement with the small far-left BSW party to form a ​government.

(Reporting by Reuters; Editing by Tom Hogue)

data.title: Ebola infections top 7,000 in Congo as virus spreads to new province
data.description:
Ebola infections top 7,000 in Congo as virus spreads to new province

Reuters
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 10:54 pm UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Congolese medical workers dressed in personal protective equipment (PPE) prepare an emergency unit at the Muthiri Adventist Hospital

1 of 2
Congolese medical workers dressed in personal protective equipment (PPE) prepare an emergency unit at the Muthiri Adventist Hospital, as aid agencies intensify efforts to contain a new Ebola outbreak involving the Bundibugyo strain in the Mutiri quarter of Butembo, North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo, September 10, 2026. REUTERS/Gradel Muyisa Mumbere

DAKAR, Sept 11 (Reuters) - The number of confirmed Ebola cases in Democratic Republic of Congo has passed ‌7,000, with the virus spreading to a new province, ‌government data showed on Friday.

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo species of ​Ebola, became the largest and deadliest in Congo's history after surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.

It is now second only to the 2014-2016 West African outbreak, which infected over 28,600 people and ‌killed more than 11,000 ⁠across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Government figures showed late on Friday that the death toll had ⁠risen to 3,398, while confirmed cases reached 7,022 across seven provinces.

Officials said earlier an Ebola case had been detected in ​South Ubangi ​province, located in the northwest ​of the country, far ‌from the epicentre of the outbreak.

They said a 23-year-old man who had died on Tuesday tested positive for the Bundibugyo species.

He left South Kivu province in eastern Congo on July 10 and spent time abroad before re-entering Congo and arriving ‌in South Ubangi, which borders ​Congo Republic and Central African Republic.

"Contact ​tracing for the first ​confirmed case in South Ubangi province is underway," ‌Congo's public health institute said ​in its latest ​situation report.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Shortages of trained staff, operational partners and funding are causing a bottleneck in efforts to expand the ​Ebola response as ‌the outbreak spreads geographically, according to the World Health ​Organization.

(Reporting by Anait Miridzhanian in Dakar; Editing by ​Nia Williams and Matthew Lewis)

data.title: Mississippi police make arrest in Tasia Fortune case after medical examiner rules death a homicide
data.description:
Mississippi police make arrest in Tasia Fortune case after medical examiner rules death a homicide

Dalia Faheid, CNN
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 10:19 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Police in Jackson, Mississippi, have arrested a man in the case of Tasia Fortune, the 29-year-old Black woman found hanging from a tree outside an abandoned house last month, following the state medical examiner ruling her death a homicide.

"Last night, the medical examiner's office officially classified Miss Fortune's death as a homicide. With that determination, our investigators moved quickly," Chief RaShall Brackney said at a Friday news conference.

Police secured two search warrants and an arrest warrant for the man, according to Brackney. After being unable to locate the man at the search warrant location, officers returning to police headquarters arrested the suspect as he was walking along a city street, she said. More arrest warrants could be served in connection with the case, the chief said.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"That arrest today is an important development in this investigation but it is not the conclusion," Brackney said.

The chief said Fortune was found in a "hanging position" with "various states of decomposition of her body" on August 3.

Fortune's death shook her family and community in Mississippi, where two other people have been found hanging from trees in less than a year.

The investigation into Fortune's death comes less than a year after the hanging deaths of 21-year-old Trey Reed, a Black student at Delta State University in Cleveland, and Cory Zukatis, an unhoused white man in his 30s, in Vicksburg, according to The Associated Press. Both deaths were determined by authorities to be suicides.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Jackson police interviewed nearly 15 people, collected forensic evidence and followed leads in the case. Brackney said the investigation into Fortune's death remains active.

"This is not closure. This is just one step as we continue to investigate this case," Brackney said.

This story has been updated with additional information.

data.title: US declares end of largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak
data.description:
US declares end of largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak

By Siddhi Mahatole
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 10:41 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Siddhi Mahatole

Sept 11 (Reuters) - U.S. health authorities on Friday declared the nation's largest recorded multistate cyclosporiasis outbreak over, after contaminated iceberg lettuce sickened thousands, though the FDA said it was still ‌probing how the parasite entered the food supply.

The outbreak, which federal investigators linked to lettuce from central ‌Mexico sourced by Taylor Farms, prompted one of the largest food recalls in recent years and renewed scrutiny of food-safety controls for imported produce.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

It ​also rattled consumer confidence, with some shoppers avoiding raw fruits and vegetables as well as dining out, hurting foot traffic at restaurants such as Taco Bell, Sweetgreen and Chipotle.

According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 12,883 people across 21 states fell ill after consuming contaminated lettuce.

The outbreak resulted in 570 hospitalizations and two deaths, and accounted ‌for more than half of the 19,595 ⁠laboratory-confirmed U.S. cyclosporiasis cases reported since May 1.

At the peak of the outbreak, before the recall, more than 1,000 infections were reported in a single day. In August, the CDC ⁠said, infections had fallen to fewer than two per day on average.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"I don't think that we have the necessary tools and technologies to stop outbreaks like this in the future," said Donald Schaffner, professor and extension specialist in food science at ​Rutgers University.

Schaffner ​called for better strain-tracking tools and sustained funding for parasite ​research to prevent such outbreaks.

The FDA said on ‌Friday it was confident that all recalled iceberg lettuce linked to the outbreak is off the market. The CDC said best-by dates for all products linked to the outbreak have passed, and the lettuce would no longer be available in stores or restaurants.

Taylor Farms recalled all iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico on July 17.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The FDA also said it had completed on-site inspections and collected samples from lettuce farms and the processing facility in Mexico, with analysis ‌pending, and will continue working with U.S., Mexican and state partners.

Taylor ​Farms, retailers Walmart, Target, Whole Foods and restaurant chains Taco Bell (Yum ​Brands), Chipotle Mexican Grill and Sweetgreen did not ​respond to Reuters requests for comment.

Michigan, the state hardest hit by the outbreak, reported more ‌than 14,000 cases and two deaths linked to ​the parasite, according to federal ​and state health officials. Ohio and Missouri also saw thousands of infections tied to contaminated lettuce from Taylor Farms.

Unusually high case totals from Michigan were attributed to a large backlog of reports processed in August, ​highlighting the strain on a system weakened ‌by federal funding cuts under the Trump administration.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Before 2026, the largest U.S. cyclosporiasis season on record ​was reported in 2019, when roughly 4,700 illnesses were documented nationwide.

(Reporting by Siddhi Mahatole, Sneha S ​K and Christy Santhosh in Bengaluru; Editing by Diti Pujara)

data.title: Arizona accuses L'Oreal of concealing cancer risks linked to hair relaxers
data.description:
Arizona accuses L'Oreal of concealing cancer risks linked to hair relaxers

By Diana Novak Jones
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 10:38 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Diana Novak Jones

Sept 11 (Reuters) - Arizona has sued L'Oreal SA and its U.S. subsidiary, alleging the cosmetics company hid evidence that its hair relaxer products could cause cancer ‌in women, as it faces thousands of similar lawsuits from users and their families.

Arizona Attorney ‌General Kristin Mayes, a Democrat, filed the lawsuit late Thursday in state court, making Arizona the first state to sue over ​alleged cancer risks linked to hair relaxers. The lawsuit accuses L'Oreal of violating state consumer protection laws by marketing the products, which are used predominantly by African American women, without warning consumers about the alleged risks of ovarian and uterine cancers.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The state is seeking penalties and damages, as well as a court order forcing ‌L'Oreal to stop selling the products ⁠unless it warns of the cancer risk.

In marketing the products to women and children over decades, L'Oreal and associated companies "exploited centuries of social pressures and discriminatory beauty ⁠standards affecting people of African descent, all while prioritizing profit over consumer safety," Arizona's lawsuit claims.

The lawsuit comes as the company faces more than 12,000 similar lawsuits filed by women or their families that have been consolidated ​in ​a Chicago federal court as part of a multidistrict ​litigation proceeding, a procedure designed to more ‌efficiently manage lawsuits filed in multiple jurisdictions.

A spokesperson for L'Oreal USA said the company is confident in the safety of its products and believes the claims are without legal or scientific merit.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

A 2022 STUDY

The products, which have been marketed under the names Dark and Lovely, Optimum and other brands, promise to permanently straighten textured hair.

The first lawsuits hit the docket after the 2022 release of a study done by ‌the National Institutes of Health that found women who used ​the products several times a year were more than twice ​as likely to develop uterine cancer.

L'Oreal's spokesperson said ​Friday the study made no finding of a causal connection between the use ‌of those products and any conditions alleged by ​the plaintiffs.

The lawsuits seek ​damages to compensate the women for their pain and suffering and economic damages for medical bills and the cost of the products, among other things.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

The lawsuits name L'Oreal, as well as ​Revlon and other makers of the ‌products. Revlon has also denied a connection between cancer and the products.

The multidistrict litigation continues ​to move forward, court records show, and trials could begin next year.

(Reporting by Diana ​Novak Jones, Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi and Aurora Ellis)

data.title: Trump and Musk super PACs unleash millions to boost Republicans in battleground races
data.description:
Trump and Musk super PACs unleash millions to boost Republicans in battleground races

By Bo Erickson and Dawn Kopecki
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 9:46 pm UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Elon Musk attend a press conference at the White House

1 of 4
U.S. President Donald Trump and Elon Musk attend a press conference in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., May 30, 2025. REUTERS/Nathan Howard

(Corrects fifth paragraph to say El-Sayed has been backed by several prominent democratic socialists, but not the group)

By Bo Erickson and Dawn Kopecki

NEW YORK, Sept 11 (Reuters) - The two biggest Republican money players in the 2026 midterm elections – U.S. President Donald Trump and billionaire Elon Musk – have finally turned on the spigot with less than eight weeks ‌to go before Election Day.

With Republicans facing the prospect of losing control of at least one chamber of Congress, and polling showing Democrats more motivated to vote, a group connected ‌to Trump has begun spending tens of millions of dollars to reserve blocks of TV ad time in close races.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump, whose approval rating is stuck at the lowest level of his political career, told reporters last week that he planned to allocate $400 million ​to $500 million to boost Republicans in the midterms.

The Trump-affiliated Republican political action committee No Going Back reserved more than $74 million in ad time this week across 15 different House races as well as Senate races in six battleground states: Alaska, Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, New Hampshire and Ohio, according to political ad research firm AdImpact. More reservations were coming in Friday afternoon, it added.

The PAC has spent the most money, $15.7 million, locking in air time in Michigan where Abdul El-Sayed, who is backed by several prominent democratic socialists, pulled ahead of Republican Mike Rogers in the polls last month, AdImpact said. One of the ads it's airing in that market ‌replays excerpts of interviews with El-Sayed in which he questioned whether police ⁠needed to carry guns and called for defunding the police. A spokesperson for El-Sayed didn't immediately return a request for comment.

Additionally, Musk's America PAC and Trump's main fundraising arm MAGA Inc. have in recent days poured $2.6 million and $10 million respectively into the race for a U.S. Senate seat in Texas where state Attorney General ⁠Ken Paxton risks becoming the first Republican to lose to a Democrat in a statewide election there in decades.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

About $7.1 million of that money is being spent on attack ads against Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico who leads Paxton by 2.1 percentage points in an average of polls compiled by Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin.

"Republicans now must spend real money defending an expanded map," said Republican strategist Brad Dayspring of Purple Strategies in Alexandria, Virginia. "When you suddenly have to ​put ​millions into Texas, having President Trump and Musk open their wallets gives Republicans the ability to shore up vulnerable ​races without draining resources from the rest of the map."

Musk's America PAC expects ‌to play a major role in Republican voter turnout efforts in key states, with spending on door knockers, digital advertising and direct-mail campaigns ahead of the November 3 election. He's already spent more than $7 million on digital advertising, text messages, voter calls, mailers and other printed materials, federal filings show. A spokesman for the PAC declined to comment.

NEW FUNDRAISING ARM

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

Trump's midterm war chest is supporting the new No Going Back super PAC, according to one person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified. It is unclear how much of Trump's war chest will be allocated through this new group.

Though Trump's MAGA Inc. and No Going Back aren't yet formally affiliated with each other, they share the same treasurer – Charles Gantt – phone number and address at the same firm in Massachusetts. Gantt, MAGA Inc. and No Going Back ‌didn't return requests for comment.

It is not clear why the new PAC, which registered with the Federal Election Commission on ​September 1, was established but Republican strategist Ron Bonjean said it helps distance Trump and his MAGA movement from campaign ​donations as voters sour on the president.

Any advertising from the new PAC will be credited to ​No Going Back PAC instead of MAGA Inc., a name closely tied to Trump's political brand.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"It's a brilliant strategy because it takes MAGA out of the name. ‌It takes any affiliation to Trump out of the name. It has an ​innocuous name that no one will care about as ​opposed to MAGA Inc., which could turn off independent voters right away," said Bonjean, a partner at bipartisan public affairs firm Rokk Solutions in Washington.

The new PAC has used some of the same vendors as MAGA Inc. to carry out its work and in August some officials from MAGA Inc. started telegraphing to Republicans their intention to create a new PAC, according to the ​person familiar with the operation.

The timing of No Going Back's registration will ‌delay full disclosure of its donors until late October, according to FEC rules.

Trump capped the first day of his Republican Party's first-ever midterm convention in Dallas on Wednesday by ​proposing to pay every U.S. adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if the party wins the congressional elections. It was not immediately clear how the $5,000 payments would work or whether they would ​be legal.

(Reporting by Bo Erickson in Washington and Dawn Kopecki in New York; Editing by Alistair Bell)

data.title: She Watched Federal Agents Kill Alex Pretti. Now She Has Told Investigators What She Saw.
data.description:
She Watched Federal Agents Kill Alex Pretti. Now She Has Told Investigators What She Saw.

Brandi Buchman
Fri, 11 September 2026 at 10:31 pm UTC
8 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Attorneys for Wynnie Savageford, a woman who watched in real time as immigration agents shot Alex Pretti to death in Minneapolis this January, revealed that she has met with the investigators from the FBI and Justice Department for a witness interview.

It's been a hard road to this moment, her attorney James Cook told HuffPost on Friday.

Politics: 'Actual Blasphemy': Critics Stunned By 'Repulsive' Video At Trump Convention

Negotiations for the interview were in the works for weeks as Cook secured immunity for Savageford so she could testify freely and without fear of retribution as the probe is underway.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"She saw him get killed. She's been freaked out by it and she's been experiencing some trauma," he said. "And these days, if you're a witness to this sort of thing, you never know if the administration is going to come after you.

The interview, Cook said, is part of the federal government's ongoing probe into Pretti's killing on Jan. 24. Savageford sat for two hours with investigators on Wednesday, and while Cook could not disclose the specifics, he confirmed that much of what she said echoed her remarks during a press conference in March.

Savageford was a legal observer of ICE officers in the Whittier neighborhood where Pretti was killed. She said agents approached her; she asked to see a warrant; they ignored her and then pushed her twice, causing her to fall. She told reporters in March that when she was tackled, agents knelt on her back and tightly handcuffed her before taking her to one of their vehicles. She said she was "picked up by my legs" and "thrown into the car headfirst."

Politics: 'You Go To Hell!': Trump Ends Convention With The Most Bizarre Pledge You'll Ever Hear

She was in the backseat of the vehicle as she watched agents kill Pretti.

Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement
Advertisement

"At that moment I thought I was going to die, too. I pleaded with agents to understand why another life was taken and please not take mine. I was told to shut the **** up and stop being hysterical," she said in March.

After Pretti was killed, Savageford, who is Asian-American, said she was taken to a warehouse near the Whipple detention center where immigrants were being detained. She was strip-searched, including by male agents who Cook told HuffPost on Friday were "touching her privates."

"They mistook her for being from somewhere south of the border and they started to process her until one of the agents said, 'Hey, she's a U.S. citizen' before they sent her off. They just assumed she was an undocumented immigrant because she's brown," he said.

Politics: Karoline Leavitt's 'Harsh Truth' At GOP Convention Comes Back To Bite Her

Once inside Whipple, Savageford says agents taunted her and asked who was "paying" her to protest.

She was released without being charged but Savageford was held for 12 hours in a freezing cell without access to food, water or a bathroom "unless you banged on the window long enough," she told reporters this spring.

Speaking of Pretti in March, Savageford said she did not know him, but knew when he went to defend her on Jan. 24 that he "had her back."

"I knew the kind of heart he had: the kind that loves and protects without limits," she said. "That day haunts me forever. That trauma will be with me for the rest of my life and I will never be the same."

Cook told HuffPost Friday that other witnesses will be interviewing with the government in the weeks ahead.

"They will probably all say the same: The agents shot Pretti and didn't know what to do. They didn't have a plan if they killed somebody. They were really coming and asking each other: 'What should we do now?' They had no first aid… when they finally called an ambulance, they really didn't know what to do," he said.

Cook said there should be "one big takeaway" about the agents involved after witness interviews are completed.

"It just seemed like they weren't well trained and it was a huge amount of incompetence," he said.

Video footage captured by bystanders on their cell phones shows officers firing at least 10 shots at Pretti, 37, in a matter of seconds. Pretti, an ICU nurse for the Department of Veterans Affairs, was filming federal agents interacting with two civilians, including when an agent appeared to push a woman to the ground. Pretti tried to put himself between them and the officers and was doused with a chemical irritant. Footage showed Pretti trying to help a woman off the ground as he continued to be sprayed. Finally, he was surrounded by multiple agents and forced to the ground.

Video shows Pretti's hands were empty when agents had him on the ground. Footage showed an agent appearing to pull a gun off Pretti's hip one second before the shooting started. The agent who removed the gun appeared to be moving away from the scene when, at the same time, another agent pulled out his own weapon and pointed it at Pretti's back. On his knees and already restrained, Pretti was then fired on four times. At least six more shots followed, according to a comprehensive timeline the New York Times completed.

Customs and Border Protection agent Jesus Ochoa and Customs and Border Protection officer Raymundo Gutierrez were later identified as the shooters.

A day after Pretti was killed, then deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche defended the conduct of ICE officers in Minneapolis, saying they were acting "humanely" when responding to aggressive anti-ICE protesters.

Pretti's execution-style killing came just weeks after Renee Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, was killed by ICE officer Jonathan Ross on Jan. 7 as she drove away from a protest. (Ross was put on a three-day leave before being moved to work in an administrative capacity in another state.)

Blanche told reporters less than a week after Pretti's death that the DOJ's civil rights division would open a probe. A separate internal investigation was also opened into Pretti's shooting by the Department of Homeland Security and the FBI. The department declined to comment.

As for Good, the Justice Department has declined to open a civil rights probe into her death and instead left it to the FBI to investigate. In April, however, as HuffPost reported, the FBI probe into Good had stalled. The FBI did not return a request for comment on Friday.

In the immediate aftermath of the shootings, state and local prosecutors said that the federal government had refused to share information or evidence with them. This prompted Minnesota to sue for access to evidence related to Pretti and Good's deaths as well as the nonfatal shooting of Venezuelan immigrant and Minnesota resident Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis on Jan. 14.

(Sosa-Celis was injured after ICE officer Christian Castro shot him in the leg. Castro was charged by state prosecutors in May with multiple counts of assault and falsely reporting a crime. After federal prosecutors similarly charged him in September, he turned himself in.)

It was not until July that the U.S. attorney's office in Minnesota began sharing key evidence with the state and local investigators, according to Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty.

Moriarty told the Associated Press that hard drives containing witness statements, police body camera video and even Good's damaged car were shared with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension.

For now, Cook wouldn't say whether Savageford or other witnesses will consider suing the government for injury or damages.

But if they do, he said, he has an inkling of what the government's response will be.

"If we do get into a litigation situation, the defense is going to need qualified immunity for every single one of those agents," Cook said.

He said he fully expects agents to respond to possible allegations by saying "I was just following orders."

"Or they will say, 'How was I supposed to know I was violating a constitutional right?'" Cook said.

Immigration agents must follow strict protocols and procedures around the use of force and firearms while on duty. Training materials obtained by HuffPost in February suggest ICE officers failed to follow even the most basic steps when it came to Good.

In his decade-plus experience as a lawyer, Cook said investigations take time and the average investigation can last a year. For every piece of evidence offered, multiple rules must be followed, and the timeline can shift, but he believes things are "moving relatively fast."

"I'm optimistic," he said. "I've sat on the other side of the table with the FBI and it's always been adversarial. This hasn't been. And I'm optimistic because of that."
